title: American Airlines 009
summary: A Douglas DC-3 crashed into wooded terrain on Glade Mountain while descending through rain and clouds on the Washington-Nashville leg of a night flight. The aircraft impacted at 3,910 feet altitude while cruising at 4,000 feet according to the last radio report. Investigation determined the probable cause was the pilot's failure to maintain safe altitude under instrument conditions combined with the company's lax flight dispatch and supervision.
probable_cause: The pilot's failure to properly plan the flight and remain at a safe instrument altitude under existing conditions of bad weather. The company's laxity in dispatching and supervising the flight contributed to the accident.

factors.evidence: While cruising and flying in a southwesterly direction, as it was descending through rain and clouds, the plane impacted wooded terrain.
Aircraft impacted wooded terrain approximately 3,910 feet above sea level while the last reported position was at 4000 feet over Pulaski, Virginia.
The pilot's failure to properly plan the flight and remain at a safe instrument altitude under existing conditions of bad weather.
A contributing cause of the accident was the company's laxity in dispatching and supervising the flight.
The plane impacted wooded summit of Glade Mountain in the Appalachian Mountains, killing 17 of the 22 occupants on board.

events.text: American Airlines Flight 009 departed New York City at 9:39 p.m. on February 22, 1945.
Aircraft reported position to Washington as leaving Washington at 12:11 a.m. on February 23 with no indication of trouble.
Last radio message from captain giving plane's position as 4000 feet over Pulaski, Virginia.
Aircraft impacted wooded terrain approximately 3,910 feet above sea level while descending through rain and clouds. Wreckage strewn over path of 450 feet.

notes: Investigation conclusions from CAB report available in text
Engine trouble mentioned by survivors but insufficient detail

title: USAAF Boeing B-17 crash on North Barrule
summary: A USAAF B-17G carrying 29 personnel and 2 pilots departed RAF Ridgewell for RAF Nutts Corner. At 10:15 the aircraft was off the northeast coast of the Isle of Man flying at 500 feet altitude. Five minutes later at 10:20, the aircraft flew into the east side of North Barrule, a 1842-foot hill, and exploded in a fireball. All 31 occupants were killed in what became the deadliest aviation accident in the Isle of Man.

factors.evidence: The aircraft was en route from RAF Ridgewell to RAF Nutts Corner but flew into the east side of North Barrule
At 10:15 the aircraft was off the northeast coast of the Isle of Man flying at 500 feet altitude, but failed to avoid the 1842-foot high North Barrule five minutes later
The aircraft flew into the east side of the 1842 ft high North Barrule and exploded in a fireball

events.text: Aircraft took off from RAF Ridgewell for RAF Nutts Corner with an estimated time of arrival of 11:00
The B-17 was off the northeast coast of the Isle of Man, flying at an altitude of 500 feet
Aircraft flew into the east side of North Barrule hill and exploded in a fireball; all 31 people on board killed

notes: Limited investigation details in available text; navigation error and loss of situational awareness inferred from flight path deviation into terrain at low altitude; no accident investigation findings documented

title: 1945 Beijing C-46 crash
summary: A U.S. Army Air Forces C-46 aircraft crashed en route from Hankou to Beijing. No details available.
